On this page

Degenerate shapes and extreme aspect ratios ​

Before this page

Hill polarization tensors for the closed forms and the cubatures, and COD tensors for the cracks.

The closed forms of the Hill, Eshelby and crack opening tensors are written for a generic shape. At the shapes where two semi-axes meet, where a spheroid becomes a sphere, a disc or a needle, or where the two acoustic roots of a transversely isotropic matrix coincide, they reach removable limits. Next to those shapes they are differences of nearly equal terms. Evaluated as written, they lose every digit there. Their derivatives fare worse: the derivative with respect to a semi-axis at the point where it meets another one, or with respect to a modulus at an isotropic point, is a limit as well, and a code that merges the two semi-axes or the two roots drops it.

This page lists those situations, says for each one what goes wrong, and how the package evaluates it instead. Every figure quoted is a relative error, measured against a reference that shares no code with the formula it checks: the nested cubature at tolerances , the same integrals in 256-bit arithmetic, and, for derivatives, ForwardDiff through the cubature and finite differences of the closed form.

SituationWhat goes wrongTreatmentAccuracy
spheroid near the sphere, isotropic matrixdivided difference of two potentialsthe potentials as the integrals they stand for 
triaxial ellipsoid with two close semi-axeselliptic integrals and their divided differencesexpansion around the spheroid
derivative where two semi-axes meetthe merged shape no longer depends on their gapshapes merged only when their derivatives coincide
spheroid in a TI matrix: sphere, coincident roots, disc, needlecancellations, a square root of zerothree regimes in the mean and squared half-difference of the roots
elliptical crack near the circle power series
a cubature under ForwardDiffNaN error estimate, dual integration boundserror norm on the values, plain bounds—
self-consistent estimate of TI classestimate rebuilt as a full tensorprojection within the class faster

The integrals behind the first four rows live in src/Core/spheroid_integrals.jl.

Where two semi-axes meet: derivatives ​

An ellipsoid whose two semi-axes are equal is classified as a spheroid (or a sphere), and its closed form depends on the shared semi-axis only. Differentiate with respect to one of the two at the point where they meet, and that closed form has nothing to give: merged, the derivative of the Hill tensor of a sphere with respect to one of its semi-axes is zero, and the derivatives along the gap of the shapes next to a spheroid are off by 100 % to 550 %, without a word.

Two semi-axes carried by ForwardDiff.Dual numbers are therefore merged only when their derivatives coincide too; otherwise the ellipsoid is triaxial, and the expansion above, exact at  , carries the derivative along the gap. The same rule classifies ellipses, cylinders and cracks. A spheroid parametrized by its aspect ratio, , keeps its two equal semi-axes constant, so it stays a spheroid under differentiation. For conduction, the derivative of the Hill tensor of a sphere of radius 1 with respect to its third semi-axis is

which the package returns to rounding. Against ForwardDiff through the cubature these derivatives agree to  , and against central finite differences of the closed form to the accuracy of the differences, to  .

A kink at the circle

depends on the ratio of the smaller semi-axis to the larger, so the roles of and swap at the circle, and has a kink there as a function of either: is smallest at the circle and grows on both sides. Its derivative at the circle is one-sided. ForwardDiff orders two dual numbers of equal value by their partials, so the semi-axis being increased is sorted as the larger one, and the derivative returned is the one in the direction of the increase. Next to the circle, it agrees with the cubature to  .

Cubatures under ForwardDiff ​

Two traps stop a cubature under differentiation.

  • The error estimate. QuadGK compares the Kronrod and Gauss estimates of each segment through a norm. LinearAlgebra.norm rescales by the largest entry and divides by it unless that entry iszero, and a dual number of value zero with non-zero partials is not iszero. On a segment where the two rules agree to the last bit, which a smooth integrand produces, the estimate comes out NaN and the integration stops with a DomainError — the derivative of the anisotropic conduction tensor of a sphere, for one. Every cubature of the package hands QuadGK the norm of the values: the refinement makes the decisions an evaluation without derivatives makes, so the value of a differentiated evaluation is that evaluation itself, and the derivatives ride on the same nodes.

  • The integration bounds. QuadGK has no rule for a dual interval: bounds taken in the number type of the crack make the derivative with respect to a crack semi-axis in an anisotropic matrix a MethodError. The bounds are plain numbers; the derivatives live in the integrand.

Self-consistent estimates of transversely isotropic class ​

The self-consistent scheme projects each iterate on the major-symmetric tensors. The products of transversely isotropic tensors that build an iterate land in the six- or eight-parameter Walpole form. Projected by rebuilding them as generic tensors, the class is lost, and the Hill tensor of a coaxial spheroid in the next iterate goes through a cubature. In the Walpole basis the major transpose swaps and and changes the sign of the major-antisymmetric , , so the projection is the five-parameter tensor

exact, and the estimate keeps its class. On a 3:1 spheroid the scheme then uses the closed form throughout: 46 µs instead of 4.2 ms, and the fixed point agrees with the one reached through the cubature at tight tolerances to  .

Where to go next ​

The next chapter leaves the ellipsoid for patterns whose inner strain is not uniform: Layered sphere solves the generalized Eshelby problem of a concentric multilayer. The closed forms treated here are those of Hill polarization tensors and COD tensors, and the self-consistent iteration that relies on them is in Self-consistent schemes.
